title: Why A Rigged Wall Clock Doubled Snacking?
description:
Experimental Chronicle — Stanley Schachter (1968): The Rigged Wall-Clock Cracker Test — Eating Because the Wall Says 6:05 PM!, grounded in Stanley Schachter (1968) (Science). Empirical findings show that in *August 1968 (Science), Columbia psychologist Stanley Schachter synthesized a startling series of experiments asking: When do humans stop eating because their STOMACH is full (internal physiological cues), and when do they eat purely because of SIGHT, SMELL, and THE WALL TIME (external environmental cues)?***.

At the circuit level, this episode examines how hypothalamus, insula, prefrontal cortex coordinate behavioral and neural responses, alongside evidence that first (Schachter, Goldman & Gordon 1968, cited in SRC1), volunteers arrived hungry, ate roast-beef sandwiches until full (or ate nothing), and then 'taste-tested' 5 bowls of crackers: internal-cue eaters naturally ate far fewer crackers after roast beef (15.0 vs 21.9), whereas external-cue/high-BMI eaters ate slightly MORE crackers on a full stomach than an empty one (18.8 vs 18.0).

Primary Peer-Reviewed Sources:
- Stanley Schachter (1968). Obesity and Eating. Science. https://doi.org/10.1126/science.161.3843.751
- C. Peter Herman, Janet Polivy (2008). External cues in the control of food intake in humans: The sensory-normative distinction. Physiology & Behavior. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.physbeh.2008.04.014
- Janet Polivy, C. Peter Herman (2017). Restrained Eating and Food Cues: Recent Findings and Conclusions. Current Obesity Reports. https://doi.org/10.1007/s13679-017-0243-1
